Chapter 2: The Gospels and the Problem of Historical Consistency
If you've ever sat down and really studied the New Testament, there’s probably a point where you notice things just don’t quite add up. Maybe you’re reading the nativity stories, and you realize Matthew and Luke just don’t tell the same tale. Or it hits you that John’s timeline for Jesus’ ministry is noticeably different from what you find in the other gospels. And then comes the surprise: Mark, which is actually the earliest gospel, doesn’t mention the virgin birth—or describe the resurrection appearances—the way the later gospels do.
But this isn’t just about little mistakes or someone forgetting a detail. These inconsistencies actually point to something much deeper. The gospels weren’t written by the same person, or even in the same place. Each one was shaped by someone with their own perspective, living in a different community, and bringing their own needs and hopes to the story. These aren’t straightforward eyewitness accounts—they’re stories that grew out of years of oral tradition, theological arguments, and the unique struggles of early Christians.
Let’s look at the story of Jesus’ trial and execution. In one gospel, the Jewish leaders are painted as the main antagonists. In another, it’s the Romans who take center stage. Even the details of who was there, what was said, and how the whole scene unfolded can change from one account to the next. And if you pay attention to what Jesus says from the cross, you’ll see those words aren’t always the same either.
Now, if you’re hoping to piece together exactly what happened, this can feel a bit like putting together a puzzle—except the pieces keep changing shape right in your hands. But maybe that’s not such a bad thing. What if, instead of treating the gospels as strict historical records, we see them as something else? Maybe they’re acts of faith, or ways of making sense of a traumatic loss. Maybe they’re even political documents, crafted to speak to different groups of people at a specific moment in history.
And when you look outside the gospels—to Roman historians like Tacitus or Jewish writers like Josephus—the picture gets even more interesting. They mention Jesus only in passing, if at all, and their stories are often filtered through secondhand information or their own cultural lens. The things they leave out—so much of what fills the gospel pages—really stands out. It suggests that the story we have was shaped as much by mythmaking and theology as by actual memory.
Here’s the thing: realizing this doesn’t have to feel threatening. In fact, it can be freeing. It gives us permission to really engage with these texts honestly, and to explore new ways of understanding where Christianity came from. The inconsistencies in the gospels aren’t just problems—they’re clues. Clues to the fascinating, complicated process by which the story of Jesus was created, shared, and passed down through generations.
